c-m3-solids.label: Cone, prism and sphere: the formulas that matter
c-m3-solids.summary: A handful of formulas cover the exam: cone slant height, prism volume, sphere and cylinder volumes.

c-m3-displace.label: Immersed solid: volume in = volume of water raised
c-m3-displace.summary: A solid dropped into a vessel raises the water by exactly its own volume.

c-m3-cube.label: Cube and cuboid: diagonal, identities and the room problems
c-m3-cube.summary: A cube's diagonal is side×√3; a cuboid's is √(l²+b²+h²). Many word problems (walls, tanks, cutting into smaller cubes) reduce to these.

c-m3-recast.label: Melted and recast into a different solid
c-m3-recast.summary: Volume is conserved when a solid is melted and recast: set the two volume formulas equal.

c-m3-flow.label: Pipes, rivers and rainfall: volume per unit time or area
c-m3-flow.summary: A flow is (cross-section area) × (speed); rainfall over an area is (depth) × (area) — both are just volumes in disguise.

c-m3-density.label: Weight, density and volume
c-m3-density.summary: Weight = volume × density; find the volume from the weight first, then the missing dimension.

c-m3-sphere.label: Sphere surface area and volume, and shapes built from a sphere
c-m3-sphere.summary: Surface area 4πr² and volume (4/3)πr³ — most sphere questions just chain one of these to another shape.

c-m3-fold.label: A flat sheet rolled or folded into a solid
c-m3-fold.summary: The sheet's own area or arc length becomes the solid's curved surface or base circumference — nothing is stretched.

c-m3-frustum.label: A cone cut by a plane parallel to its base
c-m3-frustum.summary: The small cone cut off is similar to the whole, so its volume scales as the cube of the height ratio.

c-m3-scaling.label: Ratio of volumes or surface areas between similar solids
c-m3-scaling.summary: Linear ratio k gives volume ratio k³ and surface-area ratio k²; go either direction with a root or a power.

c-m3-compare.label: Different solids on the same base and height
c-m3-compare.summary: Cone, hemisphere and cylinder sharing a base and height always compare as 1 : 2 : 3 in volume — a fact worth knowing outright.

c-m3-pctchange.label: Percentage change in volume or surface area
c-m3-pctchange.summary: Scaling every linear dimension by a factor k scales volume by k³ and surface area by k²; independent changes multiply like in 2D.

c-m3-polyhedra.label: Tetrahedron, pyramid and prisms with a special base
c-m3-polyhedra.summary: A regular tetrahedron's volume and surface area reduce to one edge length; a prism's volume is always base area × height, whatever the base's shape.

c-m3-nested.label: One solid inscribed in another, inscribed in a third
c-m3-nested.summary: Chain the 'fits exactly inside' conditions one at a time: each gives one shared length.

q-m3-cone.label: Slant height, radius, height or curved area of a cone
q-m3-cone.summary: Two of radius, height, slant height, volume and curved area are known; find another (Pythagoras, or the volume formula).

q-m3-prism.label: Prism or cuboid volume after a change
q-m3-prism.summary: Base area and height give the volume; a height change scales it.

q-m3-displace.label: Sphere dropped into a cylinder of water
q-m3-displace.summary: Sphere volume equals cylinder volume of the water rise; solve for whichever of the two radii or the rise is unknown.

q-m3-cube-diagonal.label: Cube: diagonal, volume and the room-diagonal word problem
q-m3-cube-diagonal.summary: Diagonal = side × √3, so volume = (diagonal/√3)³. A room's floor area gives the side directly.

q-m3-cuboid-tsa-diagonal.label: Cuboid diagonal from two edges and the total surface area
q-m3-cuboid-tsa-diagonal.summary: TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl) gives the missing edge; then diagonal² = l²+b²+h².

q-m3-identity.label: A symbolic identity linking volume and face areas
q-m3-identity.summary: If x, y, z are the areas of three adjacent faces, then v² = xyz.

q-m3-euler.label: Vertices, edges and faces of a solid
q-m3-euler.summary: v − e + f = 2 for any simple convex polyhedron — cuboid, prism or pyramid alike.

q-m3-cut-cubes.label: A cuboid cut into the fewest (or a given number of) equal cubes
q-m3-cut-cubes.summary: The biggest cube that divides a cuboid exactly has side = HCF of the three edges.

q-m3-ratio-dims.label: Edges in a given ratio, one absolute measurement given
q-m3-ratio-dims.summary: Write the edges as kx, and use the one absolute fact (surface area, volume, …) to solve for x first.

q-m3-walls.label: Area of the four walls of a room
q-m3-walls.summary: Four-walls area = 2(length + breadth) × height — a perimeter times a height, nothing more.

q-m3-tank.label: A tank's floor area, or the rise when water is poured in
q-m3-tank.summary: Volume = floor area × height (or rise); any one of the three follows from the other two.

q-m3-recast.label: One or more solids melted and recast into another shape
q-m3-recast.summary: Total volume before = total volume after (minus any stated loss); write both sides' volume formulas and solve for the unknown length.

q-m3-flow-rate.label: Volume flowing per unit time through a pipe or a river
q-m3-flow-rate.summary: Volume per second = cross-section area × speed; multiply by the time asked and convert units.

q-m3-rainfall.label: Rainfall collected over an area, or poured into a pool
q-m3-rainfall.summary: Volume of rain = depth × ground area; if it's then collected in a vessel, divide by the vessel's base area for the rise.

q-m3-density.label: A sheet or plate's dimension from its weight and density
q-m3-density.summary: Volume = weight ÷ density; then use the known shape (e.g. a thin square plate) to get the missing length.

q-m3-sphere-basic.label: Sphere: surface area, volume, radius or diameter
q-m3-sphere-basic.summary: Surface area = 4πr², volume = (4/3)πr³ — either one gives r, and so the other and the diameter.

q-m3-hemisphere-cone.label: A hemisphere recast into a cone of the same radius
q-m3-hemisphere-cone.summary: (2/3)πR³ = (1/3)πR²H gives H = 2R directly — no numbers needed.

q-m3-fold-box.label: Corners cut from a rectangular sheet, folded into an open box
q-m3-fold-box.summary: The cut square's side becomes the box's height; the sheet's remaining length and breadth shrink by twice that.

q-m3-fold-cone.label: A sector or semicircle rolled into a cone
q-m3-fold-cone.summary: The sheet's radius becomes the cone's slant height; its arc length becomes the cone's base circumference.

q-m3-frustum.label: Volume ratio when a cone is cut parallel to its base
q-m3-frustum.summary: A cut at height ratio k from the apex gives a small cone of volume k³ of the whole; the frustum below is the rest.

q-m3-scaling.label: Volume ratio to surface-area ratio, or edge/radius ratio
q-m3-scaling.summary: Volume ratio k³ ⟺ linear ratio k ⟺ surface-area ratio k² — convert between any two.

q-m3-compare.label: Cone, hemisphere, cylinder on the same base and height
q-m3-compare.summary: Volumes compare as 1 : 2 : 3; curved-surface comparisons need the slant height or hemisphere's own formula.

q-m3-pctchange.label: Percentage change in volume or surface area from a dimension change
q-m3-pctchange.summary: Volume scales with the product of all three linear-change multipliers; surface area with the product of the two that matter for that formula.

q-m3-tetrahedron.label: Volume or surface area of a regular tetrahedron
q-m3-tetrahedron.summary: Edge a: volume = a³/(6√2), total surface area = √3 × a².

q-m3-pyramid.label: Volume or total surface area of a right pyramid
q-m3-pyramid.summary: Volume = ⅓ × base area × height; TSA = base area + lateral area (triangles using the slant height to the base edge).

q-m3-prism-triangle.label: A prism whose base is a triangle given by its inradius or sides
q-m3-prism-triangle.summary: Base area = inradius × semi-perimeter, or Heron's formula from the three sides; then volume/TSA follow as usual.

q-m3-prism-quad.label: A prism whose base is a quadrilateral
q-m3-prism-quad.summary: Split the quadrilateral into two triangles with a diagonal, find each area, add; lateral area = base perimeter × height.

q-m3-nested.label: A sphere inscribed in one cube, circumscribing another
q-m3-nested.summary: The big cube's edge = the sphere's diameter; the small cube's diagonal = the same diameter, so its edge is that diameter ÷ √3.

formulas.text: Cone: l² = r² + h²     V = ⅓πr²h     curved area = πrl
Prism / cylinder: V = base area × height     Cylinder: V = πr²h
formulas.note: Height up 25% means volume × 1.25 with the same base.

formulas.text: Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³     surface = 4πr²
Sphere in cylinder: (4/3)πr³ = πR² × (rise)
formulas.note: π cancels from both sides.

formulas.text: Cube: diagonal = a√3, V = a³     Cuboid: diagonal = √(l²+b²+h²), TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl)
formulas.note: (l+b+h)² − diagonal² = 2(lb+bh+hl), a quick way to TSA when only the sum and the diagonal are given.

formulas.text: If x, y, z are the areas of three adjacent faces of a cuboid and v its volume, then v² = xyz
Euler's formula: vertices − edges + faces = 2, for any simple convex polyhedron
formulas.note: Cuboid: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. Triangular prism: 6 − 9 + 5 = 2.

formulas.text: The largest cube that exactly divides an l×b×h cuboid has side = HCF(l,b,h); the count is (lbh) ÷ side³
formulas.note: 6,9,12 → HCF 3 → 24 cubes of side 3.

formulas.text: Four walls of a room = 2(length + breadth) × height
formulas.note: It's just the base's perimeter times the height — no floor or ceiling included.

formulas.text: Tank/room volume = floor area × height; pouring in a known volume raises the level by volume ÷ base area
formulas.note: Keep every length in the same unit before dividing.

formulas.text: Melting and recasting conserves volume: sum of the volumes melted (minus any stated loss) = volume of the new solid
formulas.note: For n identical spheres recast into one: R³ = n × r³ (and the reverse, for splitting one into several).

formulas.text: Flow rate = cross-section area × speed     Volume in time t = flow rate × t     Rainfall volume = depth × ground area
formulas.note: 1 m³ = 1,000 litres; keep every length in the same unit before multiplying.

formulas.text: Weight = volume × density, so volume = weight ÷ density
formulas.note: A thin plate of thickness t and side x has volume x²t — solve for x once the volume is known.

formulas.text: Hemisphere recast into a cone of the same base radius R: (2/3)πR³ = (1/3)πR²H ⟹ H = 2R
formulas.note: No numbers are needed — it's a fixed ratio.

formulas.text: A sector of radius l rolled into a cone: l becomes the slant height, and the sector's arc length becomes the base circumference 2πr
formulas.note: A semicircle of radius l gives arc = πl, so the cone's base radius is l/2.

formulas.text: A cone cut by a plane parallel to its base at height ratio k from the apex: the small cone's volume is k³ of the whole; the piece below (the frustum) is the remaining (1 − k³)
formulas.note: A volume ratio of 1:26 between pieces means the small cone is 1/27 of the whole, so k = 1/3.

formulas.text: Similar solids: linear ratio k ⟺ surface-area ratio k² ⟺ volume ratio k³
formulas.note: Go from a volume ratio to a surface ratio via the linear ratio: take a cube root, then square.

formulas.text: Cone, hemisphere, cylinder of the same base radius r and the same height h = r: volumes are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3
formulas.note: (⅓)πr³ : (⅔)πr³ : πr³ = 1 : 2 : 3.

formulas.text: If each linear dimension changes by its own multiplier, volume scales by the product of all the multipliers that matter, and surface area by the product of the ones in that face's formula
formulas.note: Radius ×0.5, height ×1.5 on a cylinder: volume × (0.5)²×1.5 = ×0.375, i.e. a 62.5% decrease.

formulas.text: Regular tetrahedron, edge a: volume = a³/(6√2)     total surface area = √3 a²     Right pyramid: V = ⅓ × base area × height, TSA = base area + lateral area
formulas.note: A pyramid's lateral area needs the slant height to the base edge, not the pyramid's vertical height.

formulas.text: A sphere inscribed in a cube: cube edge = sphere diameter. The same sphere circumscribing a smaller cube: that cube's space diagonal = sphere diameter, so its edge = diameter/√3
formulas.note: Volume ratio (small cube : big cube) = 1 : 3√3.

q-m3-cone.cue: 'A right circular cone has radius … and height …. Slant height?' or 'volume … and height …, find the curved surface area'.
q-m3-cone.standard: l = √(9² + 40²) = √(81 + 1600) = √1681 = 41 cm. If volume and height are given instead, find r from V=⅓πr²h first, then CSA = πrl with l from Pythagoras.
q-m3-cone.fast: Recognise the triple 9–40–41; no squaring needed.
q-m3-cone.eliminate: The slant height is just over the height (40) because the radius is small: l is between 40 and 49. Only 41 is just above 40.
traps: Adding radius and height (49).
Giving the height of 40 as the slant height.
Using the volume formula with a ⅓ instead of Pythagoras.

q-m3-prism.cue: A base area and a height, and the height changes by a percentage.
q-m3-prism.eliminate: Volume must rise by exactly 25% from 432, so it is above 432 and below 600. Strike 432 (no change).
traps: Giving the original volume 432.
Adding 25 cm instead of 25%.
Using the ⅓ factor of a pyramid.

q-m3-displace.cue: 'A solid sphere is completely immersed in a cylindrical vessel…water level rises by…'.
q-m3-displace.standard: (4/3)π × 6³ = πR² × 4, so 288 = 4R², R² = 72, R = 6√2 cm. If instead the rise is unknown: (4/3)πr³ = πR² × rise, solve for the rise.
q-m3-displace.fast: Volume of the sphere ÷ rise = πR²: 288 ÷ 4 = 72 gives R² = 72 = 36 × 2.
q-m3-displace.eliminate: Check the sign of what's missing: a bigger cylinder radius means a smaller rise for the same sphere, and vice versa.
traps: Forgetting the 4/3 factor.
Using the sphere's radius as the cylinder's radius.
Leaving a squared quantity without taking the root when the radius itself was asked.

q-m3-cube-diagonal.cue: 'The diagonal of a cube is …. Find its volume', or 'the floor area of a cubical room is …, find the longest rod that fits inside'.
q-m3-cube-diagonal.standard: Side = diagonal/√3, then volume = side³. From a floor area A: side = √A, diagonal = side√3.
q-m3-cube-diagonal.fast: Volume = diagonal³/(3√3) in one line, skipping the side as an intermediate value.
q-m3-cube-diagonal.eliminate: The volume must be noticeably smaller than diagonal³ (since side < diagonal) — rules out any option close to or above it.
traps: Using diagonal² instead of diagonal²/3 when finding the side squared.
Confusing the face diagonal (a√2) with the space diagonal (a√3).
Giving the side instead of the volume, or the reverse.

q-m3-cuboid-tsa-diagonal.cue: 'Two adjacent sides of a cuboid are … and …, and its total surface area is …. Find the diagonal', or 'l+b+h = … and the diagonal is …, find the TSA'.
q-m3-cuboid-tsa-diagonal.standard: From TSA and two edges, solve 2(lb+bh+hl)=TSA for the third edge, then diagonal²=l²+b²+h². Going the other way: TSA = (l+b+h)² − diagonal².
q-m3-cuboid-tsa-diagonal.fast: (l+b+h)² − diagonal² skips finding l, b, h individually whenever their sum is already given.
q-m3-cuboid-tsa-diagonal.eliminate: The diagonal must be longer than the longest single edge but shorter than the sum of all three — a quick sanity check.
traps: Using only two of the three cross-terms in the TSA formula.
Forgetting to square the sum (l+b+h) before subtracting the diagonal squared.
Mixing up the face diagonal with the space diagonal.

q-m3-identity.cue: 'The areas of three adjacent faces of a cuboid are x, y, z and its volume is v. Which relation holds?'
q-m3-identity.standard: x=lb, y=bh, z=hl, so xyz = l²b²h² = v². Hence v² = xyz.
q-m3-identity.fast: Plug in any easy cuboid (2,3,4) to check which printed relation actually holds — faster than deriving it from scratch under pressure.
q-m3-identity.eliminate: Units must match: v is a volume (length³), so only a relation matching v² against three areas multiplied (length⁶) can be dimensionally right.
traps: Guessing v³ = xyz by analogy with volume being 'cubic'.
Mixing up which faces are 'adjacent' (they must share an edge, so their product uses each dimension exactly twice).

q-m3-euler.cue: 'If v, e, f are the vertices, edges and faces of a [cuboid/prism/...], find v − e + f' or a variant like (v+e−f)/2.
q-m3-euler.standard: v − e + f = 2 always, for any simple convex solid. Substitute into whatever combination is asked.
q-m3-euler.fast: Just count v, e, f for the named solid directly (cuboid: 8,12,6; triangular prism: 6,9,5) and plug into the given expression — no need to re-derive Euler's formula itself.
q-m3-euler.eliminate: Whatever combination is asked, it collapses to a fixed small number (2, or 2 divided by something) regardless of the solid's size.
traps: Sign errors in v − e + f.
Counting a square pyramid's or prism's vertices/edges/faces incorrectly.
Treating the expression as depending on the solid's dimensions, when it's purely topological.

q-m3-cut-cubes.cue: 'A cuboid of dimensions … × … × … is cut into the least number of equal cubes', or 'cut into cubes of edge …, how many?'
q-m3-cut-cubes.standard: For the LEAST number: side = HCF of the three edges, count = volume ÷ side³. For a GIVEN edge: count = volume ÷ (given edge)³ directly, provided it divides evenly.
q-m3-cut-cubes.fast: HCF(6,9,12)=3 jumps straight to the answer without listing factors.
q-m3-cut-cubes.eliminate: The count must be a whole number — if dividing volume by the cube's volume doesn't come out exact, the wrong edge was used.
traps: Using the LCM instead of the HCF for the 'least number of cubes' version.
Forgetting to cube the chosen edge before dividing.
Mixing up which cuboid dimensions were given.

q-m3-ratio-dims.cue: 'The edges of a cuboid are in the ratio … : … : … and its [surface area / volume] is …. Find its [volume / a particular edge].'
q-m3-ratio-dims.standard: Write the edges as kx, (k₂)x, (k₃)x. Substitute into the given absolute fact (TSA or volume) to solve for x, then compute whatever's asked.
q-m3-ratio-dims.fast: TSA in terms of x usually has every term carrying x², so it reduces to one clean equation for x² — solve that before taking the root.
q-m3-ratio-dims.eliminate: x must come out as a whole number (or a very simple fraction) for a clean exam question — if it doesn't, recheck the ratio was substituted correctly.
traps: Treating the ratio numbers as the actual edge lengths.
Forgetting the factor of 2 in the surface-area formula.
Using the wrong pair of ratio parts for the term that needed them.

q-m3-walls.cue: 'The area of the four walls of a room is …, its length is … times its breadth, and its height is …. Find the floor area.'
q-m3-walls.standard: 2(l+b)×h = given wall area. Substitute l in terms of b (from the given ratio), solve for b, then l, then floor area = l×b.
q-m3-walls.fast: Divide the wall area by (2×height) first to get (l+b) directly, before worrying about the ratio.
q-m3-walls.eliminate: The floor area must be noticeably smaller than (wall area), since walls scale with height too — a rough bound rules out oversized options.
traps: Including the floor and ceiling in the 'four walls' area.
Using breadth where length was meant in the given ratio.
Forgetting to multiply by 2 for the two pairs of opposite walls.

q-m3-tank.cue: 'The volume of air in a room is …, its height is …, find the floor area', or 'a tank is half full; … litres more are poured in; by how much does the level rise?'
q-m3-tank.standard: Floor area = volume ÷ height directly. For a level-rise question: convert the poured volume to the same unit as the tank's dimensions, then divide by the base area.
q-m3-tank.fast: 1 litre = 1,000 cm³ = 0.001 m³ — convert once at the start and the rest is a single division.
q-m3-tank.eliminate: The rise must be small if the base area is large relative to the poured volume — sanity-check the order of magnitude before picking an option.
traps: Forgetting the litres-to-cubic-metres conversion.
Dividing by the full tank's volume instead of just the base area.
Ignoring that the tank was already half full (when that matters for a different version of the question).

q-m3-recast.cue: '…solid(s) are melted and recast into…', with or without a stated loss of material.
q-m3-recast.standard: Write the total volume before (sum of the melted solids' volumes, minus any stated loss) and set it equal to the new solid's volume formula; solve for the unknown length.
q-m3-recast.fast: For spheres specifically, work directly in cubes of the radii — the 4/3 and π cancel from both sides.
q-m3-recast.eliminate: The new single solid's characteristic length must be bigger than any one of the original pieces alone (since it holds all their volume) but smaller than their simple sum.
traps: Forgetting to subtract a stated loss of material before setting up the equation.
Adding the radii/edges directly instead of their cubes.
Leaving π or 4/3 in the final answer when they should have cancelled.

q-m3-flow-rate.cue: 'Water flows through a pipe of diameter … at … cm/s. How many litres pumped in one hour?' or 'a river … m deep, … m wide, flowing at … km/h — how much water reaches the sea per minute?'
q-m3-flow-rate.standard: Cross-section area (πr² for a pipe, depth×width for a river) × speed = volume per unit time; multiply by the time asked and convert to litres (×1,000 per m³) if needed.
q-m3-flow-rate.fast: Convert the speed to the same time unit as the question first (km/h to m/min, say), so only one multiplication remains.
q-m3-flow-rate.eliminate: A pipe's flow in litres per hour is usually in the thousands, not the millions — a wrong unit conversion often overshoots by a factor of 60 or 1,000.
traps: Using diameter instead of radius in the pipe's cross-section.
Forgetting to convert km/h into the same unit as the depth and width.
Missing the final litres conversion (×1,000 per cubic metre).

q-m3-rainfall.cue: '… cm of rain falls over … hectares/km² of land', possibly followed by '… % of it is collected into a pool of base … — find the rise in level.'
q-m3-rainfall.standard: Rain volume = depth (in metres) × ground area (in m²). If collected into a smaller vessel, divide the (possibly reduced, if a percentage is lost) volume by the vessel's base area for the rise.
q-m3-rainfall.fast: 1 hectare = 10,000 m² — convert the ground area to m² immediately so the rest is pure arithmetic.
q-m3-rainfall.eliminate: The rise in a small pool is always far bigger than the original rainfall depth — don't accidentally give back the original few cm as the final answer.
traps: Forgetting to convert the rainfall depth from cm to metres before multiplying by an area in m².
Skipping the percentage-collected step when one is given.
Using the ground area again instead of switching to the pool's base area for the rise.

q-m3-density.cue: 'A square plate of thickness … and side x weighs …; 1 cm³ of the material weighs …. Find x.'
q-m3-density.standard: Volume = weight ÷ density. For a square plate of thickness t: volume = x² × t, so x = √(volume/t).
q-m3-density.fast: Convert the thickness to cm before dividing, since the density is usually given per cm³.
q-m3-density.eliminate: x² must come out to a clean perfect square for an exam question — if it doesn't, recheck the thickness unit conversion.
traps: Leaving the thickness in millimetres while the density is per cm³.
Dividing by density instead of multiplying weight by it, or the reverse.
Forgetting to take the square root after finding x².

q-m3-sphere-basic.cue: 'The surface area of a sphere is …. Find its diameter/volume', or 'volume equals surface area numerically — find the radius.'
q-m3-sphere-basic.standard: From SA = 4πr², get r² then r; diameter = 2r. For 'volume numerically equals surface area': (4/3)r³ = 4r² ⟹ r = 3 (the π cancels entirely since both sides have it).
q-m3-sphere-basic.fast: Spotting that π cancels completely in the 'volume = surface area numerically' version skips a lot of arithmetic.
q-m3-sphere-basic.eliminate: A sphere's volume-equals-surface-area radius is always exactly 3 units, regardless of what unit convention the question uses — a fact worth just remembering.
traps: Forgetting the 4/3 factor when comparing volume to surface area.
Confusing radius with diameter in the final answer.
Leaving π in an answer that should have cancelled.

q-m3-hemisphere-cone.cue: 'A hemisphere is melted and recast into a cone with the same base radius R. Express the cone's height H in terms of R.'
q-m3-hemisphere-cone.standard: (2/3)πR³ = (1/3)πR²H. The π and one R² cancel, leaving H = 2R immediately.
q-m3-hemisphere-cone.fast: No numbers are even needed — it's always exactly double, by the 2/3-to-1/3 ratio of the two volume formulas.
q-m3-hemisphere-cone.eliminate: The cone must be taller than the hemisphere's own radius (since it has to hold the same volume in a narrower shape) — rules out H=R or H=(2/3)R outright.
traps: Mixing up which formula has the 1/3 and which has the 2/3.
Treating the hemisphere's 'height' (which equals R) as the cone's height.
Introducing an unnecessary numeric radius when the relationship is purely symbolic.

q-m3-fold-box.cue: 'A rectangular sheet of … by … cm. Equal squares of side … are cut from the corners and the rest folded into an open box. Find the volume.'
q-m3-fold-box.standard: New length = original length − 2×(cut square's side); new breadth likewise; height = the cut square's side. Volume = new length × new breadth × height.
q-m3-fold-box.fast: Subtract twice the cut size from both the length and breadth before multiplying — it's the same shrink on each.
q-m3-fold-box.eliminate: The new length and breadth must each still be positive — rules out a cut size anywhere near half the shorter original side.
traps: Subtracting the cut size only once instead of twice (forgetting it's removed from both ends).
Using the cut square's side as a length or breadth instead of the height.
Mixing up which original side is the length and which the breadth.

q-m3-fold-cone.cue: 'A semicircular/sector sheet of radius … is folded/rolled to form a cone. Find its [depth / volume].'
q-m3-fold-cone.standard: The sheet's radius becomes the cone's slant height l. Its arc length (πl for a semicircle) becomes the cone's base circumference 2πr, giving the base radius; height follows from Pythagoras.
q-m3-fold-cone.fast: A semicircle always gives base radius = l/2 — a shortcut worth remembering outright.
q-m3-fold-cone.eliminate: The cone's height must be less than its slant height — rules out any option at or above the sheet's own radius.
traps: Using the sheet's radius as the cone's base radius instead of its slant height.
Forgetting that only half the full circle's circumference becomes the arc, for a semicircular sheet.
Skipping the final Pythagoras step from slant height and base radius to the cone's height.

q-m3-frustum.cue: 'A cone of height … is cut by a plane parallel to its base so that the small cone's volume is a given fraction of the whole. At what height is the cut made?'
q-m3-frustum.standard: If the small cone (cut off at the top) is a fraction f of the whole volume, its height from the apex is (f)^(1/3) × total height. The cut's height above the BASE is (total height) minus that.
q-m3-frustum.fast: Cube-root the volume fraction first — a fraction like 1/27 instantly gives a linear ratio of 1/3.
q-m3-frustum.eliminate: Be careful whether the question wants the height measured from the apex or from the base — they add up to the cone's total height.
traps: Measuring from the base when the apex was meant, or the reverse.
Taking the square root of the volume fraction instead of the cube root.
Confusing the 'small cone's volume' fraction with the 'remaining frustum's volume' fraction.

q-m3-scaling.cue: 'The volumes of two [similar solids] are in the ratio … : …. Find the ratio of their surface areas (or edges/radii).'
q-m3-scaling.standard: Take the cube root of the volume ratio to get the linear ratio, then square that for the surface-area ratio (or just state the linear ratio if that's what's asked).
q-m3-scaling.fast: If the volume ratio is already a perfect cube ratio (like 8:27 = 2³:3³), the linear ratio is read off immediately.
q-m3-scaling.eliminate: A surface-area ratio must be 'closer to 1' than the corresponding volume ratio (since squaring a ratio of similar-sized numbers moves it less than cubing does) — rules out any option more extreme than the volume ratio itself.
traps: Squaring the volume ratio directly instead of first taking the cube root.
Mixing up which ratio (volume, surface area, or linear) is being asked for.
Forgetting π cancels when it's the same shape on both sides, so it never needs to appear in the final ratio.

q-m3-compare.cue: 'A cone, a hemisphere and a cylinder stand on equal bases and have equal heights. Find the ratio of their volumes (or curved surfaces).'
q-m3-compare.standard: Volumes are always 1 : 2 : 3 for cone : hemisphere : cylinder (height = radius in all three). For curved surfaces, compute each directly: cone needs its own slant height.
q-m3-compare.fast: Memorise 1:2:3 for the volume version outright — it never changes with the actual radius.
q-m3-compare.eliminate: The hemisphere's curved surface (2πr²) is always exactly √2 times the cone's (πrl, with l=r√2 when height=radius) — a quick cross-check for the CSA version.
traps: Assuming the 1:2:3 volume fact also applies to curved-surface-area questions (it doesn't — CSA needs its own derivation).
Mixing up which solid is listed first/second/third in the ratio asked.
Forgetting the cone's height here equals its radius, which is what makes 1:2:3 come out so cleanly.

q-m3-pctchange.cue: 'The radius of a cylinder is decreased by …% and its height increased by …%. Find the % change in volume', or 'each edge of a cube is increased by …%, find the % change in surface area.'
q-m3-pctchange.standard: Multiply the relevant multipliers together (squared for the two dimensions in a radius², cubed if all three matter for volume) and convert the result to a percentage change.
q-m3-pctchange.fast: For 'each edge/dimension changes by the same %', volume's multiplier is (1+x/100)³ and surface area's is (1+x/100)² — just plug in.
q-m3-pctchange.eliminate: A decrease in radius dominates a volume change more than an equal-sized increase in height, since radius appears squared — so a 50%-radius-decrease, 50%-height-increase combination must still net to a decrease.
traps: Adding percentages instead of multiplying the factors.
Using the wrong power (squared when cubed was needed, or the reverse) for volume vs. surface area.
Dropping the sign on a decrease before multiplying.

q-m3-tetrahedron.cue: 'The length of each edge of a regular tetrahedron is …. Find its volume (or total surface area).'
q-m3-tetrahedron.standard: Volume = a³/(6√2); total surface area = √3 × a² (four equilateral faces of side a).
q-m3-tetrahedron.fast: Both formulas need only the one edge length — substitute directly, no intermediate steps.
q-m3-tetrahedron.eliminate: The surface area (in terms of a²) and the volume (in terms of a³) must simplify to numbers with a clean √2 or √3 factor respectively — a mismatched surd in an option is a giveaway it's wrong.
traps: Confusing the tetrahedron's volume formula with a general pyramid's (⅓×base×height), which needs the height found separately.
Using √2 where √3 was needed, or the reverse, between the volume and surface-area formulas.
Forgetting a regular tetrahedron has 4 faces, not fewer.

q-m3-pyramid.cue: 'A right pyramid has a square/rectangular base of side …; its volume is …. Find its height', or 'base side … and height …; find the total surface area.'
q-m3-pyramid.standard: Height from volume: h = 3×V ÷ base area. TSA: find the slant height to a base edge via Pythagoras (vertical height and half the base side), then TSA = base area + 4×(½×base edge×slant height).
q-m3-pyramid.fast: Check whether the 'slant height' needed is to an edge's midpoint or to a corner — most of these are the simpler edge-midpoint version, which only needs half the base side.
q-m3-pyramid.eliminate: The pyramid's slant height must be longer than its vertical height — rules out any TSA computed with the wrong one.
traps: Using the vertical height directly as the slant height in the TSA formula.
Forgetting the factor of 3 (or its absence) when switching between V=⅓×base×height and solving for height.
Mixing up the square base's side with its diagonal.

q-m3-prism-triangle.cue: 'A right prism has height … and a triangular base with sides …', or 'the base's perimeter is … and its inradius is …, and the prism's volume is …. Find the height (or total surface area).'
q-m3-prism-triangle.standard: Base area via inradius × semi-perimeter, or via Heron's formula from the three sides (check for a right triangle first). Then volume = base area × height, and TSA = 2×base area + perimeter×height.
q-m3-prism-triangle.fast: Recognise a 9-12-15 (or other scaled 3-4-5) right-triangle base instantly — area is just ½×leg×leg, skipping Heron's formula.
q-m3-prism-triangle.eliminate: The lateral surface area (perimeter × height) is usually the dominant part of the TSA for a tall, thin prism — a sanity check on the two terms' relative size.
traps: Using the triangle's perimeter where its area was needed (or the reverse).
Forgetting to double the base area in the TSA formula (there are two triangular ends).
Missing a right-angled base, leading to unnecessary Heron's-formula arithmetic that invites slips.

q-m3-prism-quad.cue: 'The base of a right prism is a quadrilateral ABCD with given sides and one right angle. Given the volume, find the lateral surface area (or the base area).'
q-m3-prism-quad.standard: Split the quadrilateral into two triangles along a diagonal; find the diagonal via Pythagoras (using the right angle) and each triangle's area via Heron's formula or ½×legs. Add for the base area; height = volume ÷ base area; lateral area = base perimeter × height.
q-m3-prism-quad.fast: The right angle given in the problem almost always marks exactly where to draw the diagonal that splits the quadrilateral cleanly.
q-m3-prism-quad.eliminate: The quadrilateral's base perimeter (needed for the lateral area) is just the sum of its four given sides — no extra computation needed there.
traps: Splitting the quadrilateral along the wrong diagonal (not using the given right angle).
Forgetting to add both triangles' areas for the full base area.
Using the base area instead of the perimeter when computing the lateral surface.

q-m3-nested.cue: 'A sphere is inscribed in a cube and circumscribes a smaller cube (or the reverse chain). Find the ratio of the two cubes' volumes.'
q-m3-nested.standard: Big cube's edge = sphere's diameter d. Small cube's space diagonal = the same d, so its edge = d/√3. Volume ratio (small:big) = (d/√3)³ : d³ = 1 : 3√3.
q-m3-nested.fast: The ratio 1 : 3√3 is fixed for this exact nested construction — worth remembering outright once derived.
q-m3-nested.eliminate: The small cube must be much smaller than the big one (its diagonal, not its edge, equals the big cube's edge) — rules out any ratio close to 1:1 or 1:2.
traps: Using the sphere's radius where its diameter was needed, or the reverse.
Setting the small cube's EDGE (rather than its diagonal) equal to the sphere's diameter.
Cubing only one side of the ratio instead of both.

pyqs.text: A sphere is circumscribed and inscribed about two different cubes respectively. Find the ratio of volume of these cubes.
solution: Big cube's edge = sphere's diameter d (sphere inscribed in it).
Small cube's space diagonal = same d (sphere circumscribes it), so its edge = d/√3.
pyqs.trick: One sphere, two different 'fits exactly' conditions: edge=diameter for one cube, diagonal=diameter for the other.
